title: Getting Started with GitOps and ArgoCD — 1
partialText:
GitOps

The discussion of GitOps almost always and naturally begins with its foundation: DevOps. The DevOps movement was born out of the need to automate application delivery, enabling the teams that write, ship, and support software to work together toward a common goal. DevOps is not necessarily a specific department; it is a culture within your organization. So, what is the relationship between GitOps and DevOps? It’s actually quite simple: GitOps is DevOps. GitOps is the natural evolution of DevOps, translating the best practices that DevOps practitioners already advocate into a standardized infrastructure practice.

When you research the term GitOps, you will likely come across many seemingly unrelated concepts. So, is GitOps a tool used by application developers, a way for infrastructure teams to manage their environments, or simply a new name for continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines?

Simply put, GitOps is a declarative methodology that treats Git as the “Single Source of Truth” for infrastructure and application management. It advocates that any configuration changes in systems like Kubernetes or Terraform should never be made manually on the servers, but exclusively by updating the code in Git. Furthermore, GitOps ensures the continuous reconciliation between this desired state defined in Git and the actual, current state of the system.

GitOps Principles

1. Declarative A system managed by GitOps must have its desired state expressed declaratively. This means instead of telling the system step-by-step “how” to operate, we define “what the final state” should be. This approach is exactly identical to the inherent declarative nature of Kubernetes itself.

2. Versioned & Immutable The desired state of the system must be stored in a way that is trackable, versionable, and immutable. The best industry standard for this principle is Git. Every configuration change is saved as a new version (commit), and past versions remain intact. This ensures the entire history of the system is preserved, allowing for safe rollbacks to a previous version when necessary.

3. Pull-Based Automation Software agents must automatically pull the desired state declarations from the source. This is exactly where GitOps diverges from traditional CI/CD processes. Instead of “pushing” changes to the system via an external trigger using a CI tool, agents periodically poll the Git repository and pull any new changes into the environment. This approach is significantly more secure as it does not require external access to the cluster. In the system architecture, tools like ArgoCD or Flux typically assume the role of this “software agent.”

4. Continuous Reconciliation The agents in the system continuously observe the “current state” of the live environment against the “desired state” defined in Git. If someone manually intervenes in the system (for example, using kubectl edit) or if any divergence (drift) is detected between these two states, the agents automatically work to synchronize the live system back to the state defined in Git. GitOps takes this reconciliation process—which Kubernetes controllers perform for single objects—and makes it continuous across the entire application and infrastructure stack.

Why Argo CD?

Traditional, event-driven (push-based) deployment methods struggled to align with the declarative nature of Kubernetes. The primary reason DevOps experts have so widely adopted Argo CD is that it perfectly complements this architecture. However, the practical advantages that truly make Argo CD an industry standard are as follows:

  • Advanced Web Interface (UI) and Visualization: Understanding what is happening behind the scenes in the GitOps world can sometimes be difficult. With its user-friendly interface, Argo CD instantly visualizes the state of resources within Kubernetes (such as Deployments, Services, Ingresses, etc.) and any differences (drift) between the Git repository and the live environment.
  • Kubernetes-Native Architecture: Argo CD is not an external server connecting to your system; it is a native component (operator) running directly within your Kubernetes cluster. This enables it to directly leverage Kubernetes’ inherent capabilities and CRD (Custom Resource Definition) structures.
  • High-Level Security (Pull-Based Model): In the past, CI/CD servers (such as Jenkins) required broad permissions (admin privileges) to deploy applications to Kubernetes. Because Argo CD runs inside the cluster and only “reads” the Git repository, there is no need to grant inbound access credentials or punch holes in your firewall.
  • Self-Healing and Fast Rollbacks: If a manual intervention occurs in the live environment (for example, someone logs into the server and messes up the configuration), Argo CD can instantly detect this and revert it to the correct state defined in Git (Self-Healing). In the event of a deployment issue, it allows you to restore the entire application to a previous stable state in seconds simply by reverting to an older version (commit) via Git, avoiding any complex rollback procedures.
  • Multi-Cluster Management: Argo CD enables you to manage not just the cluster where it is installed, but dozens of different Kubernetes clusters simultaneously from a single, centralized control plane.

Introduction to Argo CD

Kubernetes has caused a major disruption in the tech industry. Its role as the cornerstone of the entire cloud-native ecosystem cannot be overstated. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) was founded with Kubernetes at its core, and as a result, numerous open-source tools have been developed around the principle of leveraging Kubernetes’ immutable and declarative nature.

As the popularity and adoption of Kubernetes grew, the cloud-native ecosystem expanded as a whole. The need to support diverse use cases paved the way for the development of Kubernetes-native projects, tools, and various initiatives required to further accelerate the adoption of Kubernetes and cloud-native architectures.

What Is Argo CD?

Argo CD is an open-source Continuous Delivery (CD) tool designed to implement GitOps principles on Kubernetes.

It operates as a controller within Kubernetes. Its role is quite simple: it continuously monitors and compares the “Desired State” defined in your Git repository against the “Live State” currently running in your Kubernetes cluster.

Argo CD Architecture

Argo CD’s architecture is designed entirely in line with the cloud-native nature of Kubernetes itself. Instead of being an externally connected server, it is installed directly inside your Kubernetes cluster as a set of Deployments and Services.

1. API Server This is the system’s gateway to the outside world. Whether you use Argo CD’s sleek web interface (UI), run CLI commands from the terminal, or send requests via a CI tool; they all communicate with the API Server first.

  • Manages Authentication processes.
  • Handles commands such as creating applications, deleting them, or triggering manual synchronizations.
  • Enforces RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) to verify what actions users or services are authorized to perform.

2. Repository Server (Repo Server) This is the component that communicates directly with your Git repositories (or Helm repos). It acts as a sort of “translator.”

  • The files you store in Git may not always be in pure YAML format (they could be Helm Charts or Kustomize configurations).
  • The Repo Server pulls these files from Git, compiles them (for example, by running helm template in the background), and converts them into pure Kubernetes manifests (YAML) that the Application Controller can understand.
  • Caches Git repositories locally to improve performance.

3. Application Controller This is the actual “brain” and workhorse of the system. It operates on the classic Kubernetes Controller logic and runs a continuous reconciliation loop.

  • Continuously monitors the current state of the live system (Live State).
  • Receives the Desired State from the Repository Server.
  • Compares these two states. If there is a difference (drift) between the code in Git and the live environment, it marks the application’s status as OutOfSync.
  • If the Auto-Sync feature is enabled, it instantly applies the updated state from Git to the live cluster.

Argo CD Installing

We will deploy Argo CD in our Kubernetes environment using Helm. To do this, you can either set up a local Kubernetes cluster on your own machine using Minikube, or you can provision one on a cloud provider. Since the main focus of this article is Argo CD, I will leave the Kubernetes installation steps to you.

First, let’s create a dedicated namespace for Argo CD on Kubernetes.

kubectl create ns argocd

First, add the Argo CD Helm repository:

helm repo add argo https://argoproj.github.io/argo-helm

Install the Helm chart using the default configuration and create a new namespace called argocd using the following command:

helm upgrade -i argo-cd argo/argo-cd -n argocd --create-namespace

Now, let’s run the following command to verify if Argo CD has been successfully installed:

kubectl get pods -n argocd

You can gain access to Argo CD by connecting to its user interface. To do this, run the following command to forward port 8081 from your local machine to the Argo CD API server service, which will grant you access to the UI:

kubectl port-forward svc/argo-cd-argocd-server -n argocd 8081:443

After running the command, you can navigate to https://localhost:8081/ in your browser to access the Argo CD UI.

Now that we have opened the UI, we need to log into Argo CD. To do this, we need a username and a password. The default username for Argo CD is admin. To retrieve the password, you need to run the following command in your terminal:

kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o \
jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d; echo

Once you log into Argo CD, you will be greeted by the following screen:

If you’ve stayed with me this far, it means we have made a solid entry into the world of GitOps and Argo CD. In the next article of this series, we will put theory into practice, dive deep into Argo CD, and deploy our very first application.

Thank you so much for reading! You can follow along to stay updated on future articles, and if you’d like to show your support, feel free to leave some claps. See you in the next post!

title: The Missing Runtime Between AI Agents and Enterprise Backends — Part 2 of 2
partialText:
From failure patterns to a working runtime: shifting the execution boundary, capabilities as code, and a practical path to production.

From failure patterns to a working runtime: shifting the execution boundary, capabilities as code, and a practical path to production.

A language model is a probabilistic system. Given the same prompt twice, it can produce different outputs, choose different tools, and take different paths through the same workflow.

That is fine for conversation. It is a problem when the same system is asked to run a payment authorization where the fraud check has to clear before the funds move, every time, without exception.

Part 1 covered ten patterns that show up when a probabilistic system is placed inside a deterministic workflow. They looked like separate problems but they came from the same architectural choice. The model was being asked to do orchestration work, and orchestration work needs guarantees that a probabilistic system cannot give.

This part is about what to do instead.

A bigger model will not save this

You might wonder if the next generation of models will absorb most of these problems on its own.

That assumption breaks against how transformer inference actually works.

A transformer computes attention over a finite context window. Every token in that window competes for attention weight against every other token. The signal-to-noise ratio of what enters the window shapes what the model can reason about.

Raw API payloads, intermediate IDs, and backend error codes drive that ratio down. A smarter model with a low signal-to-noise context still attends to noise. A longer context window does not help. It gives the model more surface over which to lose focus, which is what the lost in the middle literature shows.

A bigger model does not fix a context engineering problem.

The rest of this piece walks through how to engineer that context: where the boundary sits, what capabilities look like in Python, how failure is handled, and how to deploy it. Start with what actually flows through the model.

Consider what flows through the model in a typical workflow.

A sanctions check returns {"pep_matches": [...], "adverse_media": [...], "shell_company_probability": 0.73}. A vendor lookup returns the full ERP record. An insurance API returns the carrier's underwriting notes.

None of that is what the model needs to do its job.

It ends up there because that is what the tool returned, and passing it back to the model was the simplest thing to do.

Data Exposure

The model does not need the raw sanctions data. It needs {"passed": false, "risk_score": 73}. The raw response is sensitive, and putting it in context creates a leak surface:

  • Prompt injection
  • Log exposure
  • Fine-tuning data extraction

Sensitive data in context is exposed. Whatever the model is, the data is reachable.

Cost

Every intermediate result in context costs tokens.

A five-step workflow with raw API responses can consume three to five thousand tokens on data the user never sees. More capable models tend to cost more per token, so plumbing data through context gets more expensive as models improve.

Audit

When something goes wrong in production, you need to know:

  • What happened
  • Who authorized it
  • What data was accessed
  • In what order

With model-driven tool orchestration, the audit trail is the conversation log, which mixes reasoning with execution and varies between runs.

In regulated environments, the auditor does not want to read the model’s chain of thought to figure out whether the sanctions check ran before the vendor record was created.

Determinism

Tool selection is non-deterministic. The same request can produce a different tool sequence on a second run. That is fine in chat. It breaks enterprise workflows where consistency matters.

Onboard Acme Corp as a supplier should run the same checks in the same order each time. If the model picks tools ad hoc, even at 99 percent accuracy, the 1 percent where it skips the sanctions check is an incident.

Tool surface growth

Loading a large tool catalog onto an agent is bad architecture.

  • Microsoft’s tool-space interference work shows that adding more tools to an agent can actively hurt performance.
  • The IBM LongFuncEval paper measured 7 to 85 percent accuracy degradation as the tool catalog grew from 8K to 120K tokens.
  • The Less-is-More paper found that reducing the available tool set cuts execution time by up to 70 percent and improves task success rates.

The model is worse at the job, not better, when you give it more to choose from.

There is also a maintenance cost. Someone has to define, version, and update every tool.. Every internal API change means a tool definition update. The surface area grows with the system.

Shifting the execution boundary

The ten failures from Part 1 share a root cause.

The model is inside the execution loop. It picks tools, sequences calls, manages state, and interprets results. That work belongs in governed runtime.

This is the problem Lattice is designed for. Lattice is an open framework I have been building for putting the execution layer back where it belongs: in code that runs outside the model.

It has two parts. The first is a runtime, an engine that sits between the agent and the backend systems it touches. The second is a code model for defining workflows. You write workflows as Python files called capabilities, each one a typed contract with declarative steps inside it.

Lattice loads those capabilities and executes them when the model asks for an outcome. What comes back is a projection: a small object containing only what the model needs to reason about and explain to the user.

The boundary has two sides. On one side, the model sees outcomes it can request and projections it can reason about. On the other side, you have ordinary Python code with explicit dependencies, retries, permissions, and failure policies.

Lattice is the layer that turns one into the other.

A few things change once Lattice owns the boundary.

  • Intermediate state stays in the runtime, and only decision-relevant data reaches the model.
  • Permissions and failure behavior live in the capability code, enforced by Lattice rather than negotiated in prose.
  • The model never decides whether to retry, never builds auth headers, never reasons about error recovery.
  • And every execution leaves behind a structured audit record you can query, not a transcript you have to parse.

The next section shows what a capability actually looks like as code.

Adding more capabilities does not grow the tool surface

The vendor onboarding example was one capability. Here are three more, from different domains:

VendorOnboarding(vendor_name, vendor_type, region)
  -> { vendor_id, status, compliance, risk_score, documents_pending }

EquipmentProcurement(item, quantity, budget_department,
                     preferred_vendor, requested_by)
  -> { order_status, total_cost, vendor_name,
       approval_status, budget_remaining }

TripPlanning(traveler_email, origin, destination,
             departure_date, return_date, department)
  -> { status, flight_confirmation, hotel_confirmation,
       total_cost, policy_status, budget_remaining, loyalty_tier }

Same shape every time. Typed inputs the model fills from the user’s request, and a small projection it can reason about. The fields inside the projection are decision-relevant. There are no backend identifiers and no internal status codes.

The implementations underneath have nothing in common.

VendorOnboarding runs five sequential steps against compliance and ERP systems. EquipmentProcurement does inventory lookups, budget checks, and approval routing, with branching on whether the requested vendor is preferred.

TripPlanning is eight steps: flight search, hotel search, loyalty lookup, policy check, approval, budget allocation, flight booking, hotel booking. Some run concurrently when they do not depend on each other. Some have soft failures with fallbacks for when an external API is down.

The model does not know about any of it. It calls TripPlanning with six inputs and gets back seven output fields, the same way it calls the other two.

This is why adding a new step inside a capability is cheap. The signature does not change, the projection does not change, the model does not need to learn anything new. You can rewrite half the steps in VendorOnboarding to use a different sanctions provider, and the agent calling it does not notice.

Two tools instead of N

Lattice exposes exactly two tools to the model, regardless of how many capabilities exist:

search_capabilities(query)        -> matching capability signatures
execute_capability(name, inputs)  -> projection

The model calls search_capabilities("vendor onboarding supplier"). Lattice searches its manifest, which holds metadata only, and returns matching signatures with their inputs, projection schemas, and examples. The model picks one. It calls execute_capability("VendorOnboarding", {vendor_name: "Acme Corp", ...}). Lattice lazy-loads the module on first call, runs the capability, and returns the projection.

What the model is actually doing on that second call is emitting an intent: run this named outcome with these typed inputs. Lattice takes the intent from there. The capability code sequences the steps, manages state, enforces permissions, retries on failure, and assembles the projection. None of that traffic touches the model.

Capabilities are code, not a contract language

What do you actually write?

A capability is a Python file. No YAML schema, no DSL, no separate manifest that drifts out of sync with the code. Decorators carry the contract. The function body carries the work.

from lattice import capability, step, state, projection
from lattice.failure import retry, soft_failure, hard_failure, abort

@capability(
    name="VendorOnboarding",
    version="1.0",
    inputs={"vendor_name": str, "vendor_type": str, "region": str},
    projection={
        "vendor_id": {"type": str, "example": "V-10001",
                      "description": "Unique vendor identifier from the ERP"},
        "status": {"type": str, "example": "active",
                   "description": "Vendor lifecycle status"},
        "compliance": {"type": str, "example": "passed",
                       "description": "Overall compliance screening result"},
        "risk_score": {"type": int, "example": 15,
                       "description": "Sanctions risk score, 0-100"},
        "documents_pending": {"type": list,
                              "example": ["W-9", "insurance_certificate"],
                              "description": "Documents still required"},
    },
)
async def vendor_onboarding(ctx):

    @step(depends_on=[], scope="compliance.read")
    @retry(max=3, backoff="exponential", on=[TimeoutError, ServerError])
    @hard_failure(on_exhausted=abort)
    async def sanctions_check():
        client = ctx.client("sanctions_screening_api")
        result = await client.check(
            entity_name=ctx.intent.vendor_name,
            country=ctx.intent.region)
        return {"passed": result.clear, "risk_score": result.score}

    @step(depends_on=[sanctions_check], scope="compliance.read")
    @retry(max=3, backoff="exponential", on=[TimeoutError, ServerError])
    @soft_failure(fallback={"verified": False,
                            "warning": "insurance check unavailable"})
    async def insurance_verification():
        client = ctx.client("insurance_verification_api")
        result = await client.verify(entity_name=ctx.intent.vendor_name)
        return {"verified": result.valid, "expiry": result.expiry_date}

    @step(depends_on=[sanctions_check, insurance_verification],
          scope="vendor.write")
    @retry(max=2, on=[TimeoutError, ServerError])
    @hard_failure(on_exhausted=abort)
    async def create_vendor_record():
        erp = ctx.client("erp")
        vendor = await erp.create_vendor(
            name=ctx.intent.vendor_name,
            type=ctx.intent.vendor_type,
            region=ctx.intent.region,
            risk_score=state.sanctions_check.risk_score,
            insurance_status=state.insurance_verification)
        return {"vendor_id": vendor.id,
                "payment_terms": vendor.default_terms}

    @step(depends_on=[create_vendor_record], scope="vendor.write")
    async def set_payment_terms():
        client = ctx.client("payments_api")
        terms = await client.set_terms(
            vendor_id=state.create_vendor_record.vendor_id,
            terms="net-30", currency="USD")
        return {"terms": terms.terms, "currency": terms.currency}

    @step(depends_on=[create_vendor_record])
    async def request_documents():
        client = ctx.client("documents_api")
        result = await client.request(
            vendor_id=state.create_vendor_record.vendor_id,
            document_types=["W-9", "insurance_certificate", "bank_details"])
        return {"documents_pending": result.documents_pending}

    return projection(
        vendor_id=state.create_vendor_record.vendor_id,
        status="active",
        compliance="passed" if state.sanctions_check.passed else "failed",
        risk_score=state.sanctions_check.risk_score,
        documents_pending=state.request_documents.documents_pending
    )

The @capability decorator declares the contract the model sees: name, version, typed inputs, projection schema.

The @step functions declare the actual work. Decorators around each step handle retries, soft and hard failure policies, and the OAuth scope the step needs.

Each step declares its dependencies too. sanctions_check has depends_on=[] and runs first. create_vendor_record waits for sanctions and insurance to finish. set_payment_terms and request_documents both depend on create_vendor_record but not on each other, so they run in parallel.

The function returns a projection built from the step results.

Because this is ordinary Python, it works with ordinary Python tools. You can set breakpoints in create_vendor_record and step through it. You can mock ctx.client in pytest and unit-test sanctions_check in isolation. You can run the whole capability in CI against stub clients.

The decorators wrap async functions and register the workflow shape with Lattice at import time, which is what lets the runtime walk the dependency graph and expose the signature to the model.

The model never sees the body.

Projection design is half the value

A capability is only as useful as what it hands back to the model.

Raw backend responses make poor projections. Status codes, internal IDs, and nested payloads tell the model that something happened, without telling it what to do about it. The model ends up explaining the error code to the user, or hiding behind something went wrong.

Lattice projections are designed as decision surfaces: small, typed objects that carry what the model needs to reason, explain, and act.

Three things have to be true for a projection to do that job.

  1. The model can explain what happened in one sentence. “That seat was just booked by someone else” instead of “error 409”. “This trip exceeds your department’s Q1 travel budget” instead of “forbidden”. The model should be able to say it without translating or guessing.
  2. The model can present what comes next. A failed step earns its place in the projection only if the projection also carries the alternatives. Concrete options the user can choose between, with enough detail for the model to describe them.
  3. The model can act on the user’s choice. Each option in the projection maps to something runnable: another capability, a parameter change, a human approval request. The model does not have to invent the next step.

Here is what that looks like for a travel policy violation:

{
  "status": "blocked",
  "reason": "policy_violation",
  "violations": [
    {"policy": "International Travel Limit",
     "threshold": 1500, "current": 1850},
    {"policy": "Q1 Travel Budget",
     "remaining": 340, "required": 1850}
  ],
  "options": [
    {"action": "request_approval", "approver": "Sarah Chen",
     "estimated_wait": "4-24h"},
    {"action": "reduce_cost", "suggestions": [
      {"change": "Downgrade hotel", "saves": 400, "new_total": 1450}
    ]},
    {"action": "split_budget",
     "personal_portion": 510, "company_portion": 1340}
  ]
}

The model reads this and says:

Your trip is blocked. It is over the $1,500 travel limit and your department budget only has $340 left. I can request approval from Sarah Chen, which usually takes 4 to 24 hours. We can downgrade the hotel to save $400, which brings you under the limit. Or you can cover $510 personally and expense the rest. What works best?

When things go wrong

There are two ways a capability can fail. Lattice treats them differently, and the model sees structured feedback in both cases.

The first is intent validation. When the model emits an intent that does not match the capability’s typed schema, Lattice rejects it before any step runs. Wrong field type, missing required input, unknown capability name, or insufficient OAuth scopes all land here.

The rejection tells the model what failed and how to fix it:

{
  "error": "Missing required input: 'vendor_type' for VendorOnboarding",
  "required_inputs": {"vendor_name": "str",
                      "vendor_type": "str", "region": "str"},
  "instruction": "Resubmit the intent with all required inputs."
}

The model can ask the user for the missing field and resubmit. No partial execution, no half-onboarded vendor sitting in the ERP.

The second failure mode is mid-execution. The intent passed validation. Steps started running. Something broke partway through

Each step in a capability declares its own failure policy.

  • A step with @soft_failure(fallback=...) continues with a fallback value when its API is unreachable.
  • A step with @hard_failure(on_exhausted=abort) stops the whole capability after retries are exhausted. Nothing downstream of an aborted step ever runs, because the dependency graph means downstream steps were waiting on it.

When a soft failure fires, the projection carries a warning so the model can surface the degraded result honestly:

{
  "vendor_id": "V-10001",
  "status": "active",
  "compliance": "passed",
  "risk_score": 15,
  "documents_pending": ["W-9", "insurance_certificate"],
  "warnings": ["Insurance verification unavailable; manual review recommended"]
}

The agent can tell the user: Acme Corp is onboarded, but insurance verification was down. Someone on compliance should verify it manually.

When a hard failure aborts, the projection explains which step failed and why. The user gets an honest description of where the workflow stopped, with enough detail for the agent to suggest what to do next.

From OpenAPI spec to running capability

Lattice ships with a CLI that uses an LLM to generate capabilities from existing API specs. It is the part I have been finding most useful in practice.

If you have OpenAPI specs for your internal APIs, the flow is:

lattice discover    # Parse OpenAPI specs (YAML or JSON) into an operation inventory
lattice match       # LLM proposes which operations group into capabilities
lattice generate    # LLM writes the actual Python capability file
lattice visualize   # Review the dependency graph as interactive HTML
lattice register    # Save the manifest so agents can find it
lattice run         # Execute with a real intent and inspect the projection

A vendor API and a compliance API, both OpenAPI:

lattice discover --spec ./vendor-api.yaml --spec ./compliance-api.yaml
lattice match --spec ./vendor-api.yaml --spec ./compliance-api.yaml \
              --domain procurement --provider anthropic
lattice generate --capability VendorOnboarding --spec ./vendor-api.yaml

The output lands in ./capabilities/VendorOnboarding.py (or wherever you point -o). It is a Python file you read and edit. The decorators, the dependency graph, the retry policies, the projection schema, all generated. You still own the file. The generator gives you a starting point; you still need to think about how each step should fail.

Before anything ships, lattice visualize --html auto renders the capability as an interactive HTML page. Steps as nodes, dependencies as edges, color-coded by status (automated, human task, gap), with data flow and permission overlays. Useful for code review.

Credentials, permissions, and audit

The model should not hold credentials.

In a tool-calling setup, the model has to. Either the system prompt tells it which auth token to use for which endpoint, in which case credentials sit in context, or middleware injects them per call, in which case you are building per-endpoint auth routing for every tool you ship.

In Lattice, credentials live in a credential store that the runtime injects at execution time. The model emits onboard this vendor as a typed intent. The agent code that hosts the model looks up the authenticated user’s scopes from its own auth system and passes them to Lattice when it invokes the capability. The model never sees an OAuth token, an API key, or a scope grant.

Permissions work at the capability level.

Each step declares the scope it needs: compliance.read, vendor.write, budget.read. When the runtime is invoked, it receives the granted scopes from the calling agent, alongside the intent. It validates the full set of required scopes before any step runs. If a step needs vendor.write and the user's session does not include it, execution fails immediately. Nothing hits an API. No partial side effects.

This shifts where the security review happens.
With 30 endpoints exposed as tools, you review 30 permission boundaries scattered across 30 tool definitions. Adding a new endpoint means adding a new tool, a new permission check, and remembering to update the system prompt. With capabilities, the review surface is the capability itself. What does VendorOnboarding access? is one answer, not thirty.

Sensitive data stays in the runtime too. The sanctions check might return PEP matches, adverse media hits, and shell-company probability scores. That stays in step state. The projection only surfaces risk_score: 73. The model never sees the underlying payload, so it cannot leak what it does not have.

Every execution produces a structured audit record: who requested it, what authority was used, which steps ran, what each step accessed, what failed, and what the result was. Queryable JSON that you can hand to an auditor without explanation.

Closing

Part 1 was the diagnosis. The model ends up doing orchestration work because someone wrapped every backend endpoint as a tool, and the agent inherited the job of sequencing, state management, error handling, and data transport. Ten failure patterns followed.

This piece walked through how to solve it.

A model that emits typed intent. A runtime that loads the right capability, executes the steps, manages state outside context, enforces permissions, retries on transient failure, and assembles a projection the model can reason about. A CLI that turns existing OpenAPI specs into capability code with an LLM in the loop. Credentials that never touch context. Audit records that are structured by default.

Yann LeCun, Turing Award winner and Chief AI Scientist at Meta, made the point “that LLMs work well in domains where language itself is the substrate for reasoning”.

Conversation, explanation, presenting options — that is the model’s home turf. Orchestration is not. The substrate there is state, permissions, and side effects, and that belongs in code that can be tested, reviewed, and audited.

Lattice is open source at https://github.com/csehammad/Lattice.

The Missing Runtime Between AI Agents and Enterprise Backends — Part 2 of 2 was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Building AI Agents with Cursor Agents SDK
partialText:
TL;DR

  • Cursor Agents SDK lets you build autonomous AI agents that live inside your IDE and understand your codebase
  • Agents can read files, write code, run bash commands, and iterate in real-time, giving them the instant feedback they need to solve problems
  • You can have a working agent in 10 lines; production systems need structured tool definitions, error handling, and proper state management
  • Best for development-time tasks: documentation, refactoring, testing, code analysis
  • Synchronous execution with 60-second timeout per action; costs $0.10–$0.50 per 10-turn session
  • Currently production-ready for most use cases; not suitable for real-time request handling

If you prefer Videos more than articles, you can check this one:

What Is Cursor Agents SDK?

Imagine an AI assistant that doesn’t just suggest changes, it actually reads your code, understands your project structure, executes what it writes, sees the results, and iterates to fix problems. That’s what the Cursor Agents SDK does.

The Cursor Agents SDK is a TypeScript framework for building autonomous AI agents that live inside your IDE. Unlike traditional agent frameworks (LangChain, AutoGPT) that run as external services with limited visibility, Cursor agents are tightly integrated with your development environment. This means they have direct access to:

  • Your entire codebase (read and write)
  • Shell commands and executables
  • File system operations
  • Real-time feedback on what they executed
  • IDE state and navigation

The key insight: agents learn through feedback loops. When an agent writes code and immediately runs it, sees the error output, and fixes it, that’s when they become powerful. Pure API-based agents can only generate text and hope it’s correct. Cursor agents can verify themselves.

This matters because:

  • Speed: An agent can refactor a module in 30 seconds instead of you spending 2 hours
  • Consistency: Agents apply rules uniformly across your entire codebase
  • Documentation: Agents generate accurate docs by reading actual code, not guessing
  • Verification: Changes are tested before being written to disk

Key Differences from Other Agent Frameworks

How It Works: The Agent Loop

When you give an agent a task, here’s what happens under the hood:

  1. AI model analyzes your prompt and the current state of your code
  2. AI model decides which tool to use (read file, run bash, write file, etc.)
  3. Tool executes and returns the result (file contents, command output, etc.)
  4. AI model sees the result and decides: Is the task done? Do I need another action? Did I hit an error?
  5. Loop repeats until the task completes or the agent gives up

Let’s say you ask: “Add type safety to src/api.ts, find all functions missing return types and add them.”

The agent might run like this:

  • Turn 1: Read src/api.ts to understand the code
  • Turn 2: Analyze the functions and identify which are missing return types
  • Turn 3: Rewrite the file with return types added
  • Turn 4: Run TypeScript compiler to verify no errors introduced
  • Turn 5: Return “Done! Added return types to 8 functions”

Each turn is a complete cycle of reasoning + execution + feedback. By default, agents run up to 10 turns before stopping. Most tasks complete in 3–6 turns.

Two key constraints to know:

  1. 60-second timeout per action: If a tool takes longer than 60 seconds (building a large project, running slow tests), it’ll timeout. Plan accordingly.
  2. Synchronous execution: Agents wait for each action to complete before deciding what to do next. They can’t fire off parallel tasks.

These constraints are intentional: synchronous execution makes agents’ behavior predictable and easy to debug.

Getting Started: Your First Agent in 10 Lines

Installation

npm install @cursor-ai/agents

For a hands-on walkthrough, check out this tutorial that covers building your first Cursor agent from scratch.

Your First Agent

import { Agent } from '@cursor-ai/agents';
const agent = new Agent({
  model: 'claude-opus-4-7',
  systemPrompt: 'You are a helpful code assistant.',
  maxTurns: 10,
});
const result = await agent.run('Explain the architecture of this project');
console.log(result);

Run this, and the agent will explore your codebase, read key files, understand the structure, and explain it to you in natural language.

Choosing your model: Cursor SDK supports multiple models including GPT-4, Claude, and other providers. Start with a mid-tier model (like Claude Sonnet) for most tasks. Use faster models for straightforward work like documentation to save on usage. Use more powerful models (like Claude Opus) only for complex reasoning tasks where quality matters more than cost.

Core Concepts: What Makes Agents Work

Tools: The Agent’s Hands

Tools are how agents interact with your codebase. Built-in tools include (for the complete list, see the SDK documentation):

  • readFile(path): Get file contents
  • writeFile(path, content): Create or modify files
  • listFiles(dir): See directory contents
  • runBash(command): Execute shell commands and see output
  • findInFiles(pattern, dir): Search across files
  • navigateToFile(path, line): Jump to specific code locations

You can also define custom tools for domain-specific work:

import { Tool } from '@cursor-ai/agents';
const calculateProjectMetrics: Tool = {
  name: 'calculateProjectMetrics',
  description: 'Analyze code metrics like lines of code, complexity',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      directory: {
        type: 'string',
        description: 'Directory to analyze',
      },
    },
    required: ['directory'],
  },
  handler: async ({ directory }) => {
    // Your implementation
    return { loc: 1500, complexity: 42 };
  },
};

agent.registerTool(calculateProjectMetrics);

Prompting: How to Talk to Agents

Agent behavior comes from two prompts:

System Prompt (gives the agent a role):

const systemPrompt = `You are an expert security auditor. Find vulnerabilities in code.
Before making any changes, explain what you found and why it's dangerous.`;

Run Prompt (gives the specific task):

await agent.run('Audit src/api/auth.ts for security issues');

The specificity spectrum:

'Fix bugs in my code'

// ✅ Better, agent knows what to look for
'Find potential race conditions in src/db/connection.ts'

// ✅ Best, agent has a clear roadmap
`Analyze src/db/connection.ts for race conditions, especially in the write() 
method when two concurrent requests update the same document. Check for:
1. Missing locks
2. Unserialized transactions  
3. Stale read issues
Provide a diff for each fix.`

The difference between a 2-turn agent and a 10-turn agent is often just how clearly you describe the task.

Vague prompts make agents explore aimlessly. Clear prompts make agents execute with purpose.

State Management: Memory Across Runs

By default, each agent run is isolated, meaning the agent doesn’t remember previous conversations. For multi-turn workflows:

const agent = new Agent({
  model: 'claude-opus-4-7',
  conversationHistory: [], // This persists between runs
  contextWindow: 8000, // Limit memory to stay cheap
});

// Run 1: Agent analyzes a function
await agent.run('What does calculateHash() do?');

// Run 2: Agent remembers and builds on the previous analysis
await agent.run('How could we optimize it for large datasets?');

This is useful for iterative refinement: agent analyzes, you give feedback, agent refines. Without conversation history, you’d need to re-provide context each time.

4. Error Handling

Agents fail gracefully:

try {
  const result = await agent.run(prompt);
} catch (error) {
  if (error.code === 'TIMEOUT') {
    // Action took too long (>60s)
    console.log('Agent timed out');
  } else if (error.code === 'TOOL_ERROR') {
    // A tool failed (file not found, bash error, etc.)
    console.log('Tool failed:', error.toolName, error.message);
  } else if (error.code === 'MAX_TURNS') {
    // Agent hit turn limit without completing
    console.log('Agent gave up after max turns');
  }
}

Building Your First Production Agent

Let’s build something real: a documentation agent that reads your codebase and auto-generates JSDoc comments for all functions. This is a task that normally takes 2–3 hours of tedious manual work. An agent can do it in 30 seconds.

Step 1: Define Tools

import { Agent, Tool } from '@cursor-ai/agents';
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

const readFileContent: Tool = {
  name: 'readFile',
  description: 'Read a TypeScript or JavaScript file',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      filePath: {
        type: 'string',
        description: 'Path to the file',
      },
    },
    required: ['filePath'],
  },
  handler: async ({ filePath }) => {
    try {
      return fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf-8');
    } catch (error) {
      return `Error reading file: ${error.message}`;
    }
  },
};

const findFunctions: Tool = {
  name: 'findFunctions',
  description: 'Find all function declarations in a file',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      filePath: {
        type: 'string',
        description: 'Path to the file',
      },
    },
    required: ['filePath'],
  },
  handler: async ({ filePath }) => {
    const content = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf-8');
    const functionRegex =
      /(async\s+)?function\s+(\w+)|const\s+(\w+)\s*=\s*(async\s*)?\(/g;
    const functions = [];
    let match;
    while ((match = functionRegex.exec(content)) !== null) {
      const name = match[2] || match[3];
      functions.push({ name, line: content.substring(0, match.index).split('\n').length });
    }
    return functions;
  },
};

const updateFile: Tool = {
  name: 'updateFile',
  description: 'Add or modify content in a file',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      filePath: {
        type: 'string',
        description: 'Path to the file',
      },
      newContent: {
        type: 'string',
        description: 'New file content',
      },
    },
    required: ['filePath', 'newContent'],
  },
  handler: async ({ filePath, newContent }) => {
    try {
      fs.writeFileSync(filePath, newContent, 'utf-8');
      return 'File updated successfully';
    } catch (error) {
      return `Error writing file: ${error.message}`;
    }
  },
};

Step 2: Create and Configure Agent

const documentationAgent = new Agent({
  model: 'claude-opus-4-7',
  systemPrompt: `You are an expert TypeScript documenter. Your task is to:
1. Analyze functions and methods
2. Understand their purpose and parameters
3. Generate JSDoc comments that are clear, concise, and accurate
Follow these rules:
- Use @param for each parameter with type and description
- Use @returns for return value documentation
- Include @example for complex functions
- Keep descriptions under 80 characters per line
- Never alter the function implementation, only add documentation`,
  maxTurns: 8,
  timeout: 30000,
});

// Register custom tools
documentationAgent.registerTool(readFileContent);
documentationAgent.registerTool(findFunctions);
documentationAgent.registerTool(updateFile);

Step 3: Run the Agent

const filePath = 'src/utils/helpers.ts';

const result = await documentationAgent.run(
  `Add comprehensive JSDoc comments to all functions in ${filePath}. 
   First list all functions, then add documentation without changing the implementations.`
);

console.log('Documentation added:', result);

What Happens When You Run It

$ node agent.ts

The agent will:

  1. List all functions in the file
  2. Read each function’s code and signature
  3. Generate JSDoc by understanding what the code does
  4. Add the documentation
  5. Verify TypeScript still compiles
  6. Return “Done: Added JSDoc to 12 functions.”

Before:

function calculateHash(data: string, algorithm: string): string {
  const hasher = createHash(algorithm);
  hasher.update(data);
  return hasher.digest('hex');
}

After:

/**
 * Computes a cryptographic hash of the input string.
 * 
 * @param data - The string to hash
 * @param algorithm - Hashing algorithm: 'sha256', 'sha512', or 'md5'
 * @returns The computed hash as a hexadecimal string
 * @throws {Error} If the algorithm is not supported
 * @example
 * calculateHash('secret', 'sha256')
 * // => '2bb80d537b1da3acb47690d7...
 */
function calculateHash(data: string, algorithm: string): string {
  const hasher = createHash(algorithm);
  hasher.update(data);
  return hasher.digest('hex');
}

The key: the agent reads the actual code, understands intent, and writes meaningful documentation, not generic placeholder comments.

Advanced Patterns: Scaling Agents

Pattern 1: Step-by-Step Refinement

For complex tasks, break them into stages and let the agent build on each:

const agent = new Agent({
  model: 'claude-opus-4-7',
  conversationHistory: [], // Agent remembers each stage
});

// Stage 1: Understand the problem
await agent.run(`Analyze src/components/Form.tsx. What re-renders too often?`);

// Stage 2: Plan the fix
await agent.run(`Based on your analysis, what changes would you make?`);

// Stage 3: Execute
await agent.run(`Now implement those changes.`);

The agent builds context as it goes. By the end, it has a complete mental model of the component and its issues.

Pattern 2: Self-Validating Code

Tell the agent to verify its own work:

const agent = new Agent({
  model: 'claude-opus-4-7',
  systemPrompt: `When writing code:
1. Implement the feature
2. Run tests
3. Check for TypeScript errors
4. Only declare success after verification`,
});

await agent.run('Add validation utilities to src/utils/validators.ts with tests');

Now instead of you testing the code, the agent tests itself. If tests fail, it sees the error and fixes it.

Pattern 3: Specialist Agents

Use multiple agents with different expertise for a code review:

const specialists = {
  security: new Agent({
    systemPrompt: 'Find security vulnerabilities. Prioritize auth, injection, encryption.',
  }),
  performance: new Agent({
    systemPrompt: 'Find performance issues. Look for N+1 queries, memory leaks, inefficient loops.',
  }),
  architecture: new Agent({
    systemPrompt: 'Evaluate architecture. Check separation of concerns, modularity, testability.',
  }),
};

const file = 'src/api/users.ts';
const [secResults, perfResults, archResults] = await Promise.all([
  specialists.security.run(`Audit ${file}`),
  specialists.performance.run(`Analyze ${file}`),
  specialists.architecture.run(`Review architecture of ${file}`),
]);

console.log('Security:', secResults);
console.log('Performance:', perfResults);
console.log('Architecture:', archResults);

Three agents, each with a specific lens, running in parallel. You get a more thorough review in 30 seconds than a human review in 30 minutes. See the SDK TypeScript API reference for more advanced agent configuration patterns.

When to Use Agents (and When Not To)

Understanding Cursor SDK Pricing

Cursor SDK uses the same token-based pricing as the IDE and runs are billed against your team’s usage dashboard under the “SDK” tag. Here’s how it works:

Auto + Composer Pool (Lower-cost for straightforward tasks)

  • Input + Cache Write: $1.25/M tokens
  • Output: $6.00/M tokens
  • Cache Read: $0.25/M tokens

API Pool (When selecting specific models)

  • Charged at the model’s native API rate
  • Teams Plans add a $0.25/M token Cursor overhead on top

Teams Plans include:

  • $20/month usage per seat
  • Same request pools and Privacy Mode rules as the IDE
  • On-demand usage available after included allocation

Typical agent session cost: Depends on the model selected. A 10-turn session with mid-tier models typically costs between $0.05 and $0.50.

Check available models in your SDK:

const models = await Cursor.models.list();
// Returns: modelId, displayName, parameters, pricing info, variants

Different models affect how quickly your included usage is consumed. Claude Opus is more expensive but better reasoning. Claude Sonnet is cheaper and faster. Use Opus when quality matters, Sonnet for routine tasks.

When agents ROI: If a task saves you 30 minutes of work, it’s worth the cost. If it saves you 2 hours, it’s definitely worth it. Most code generation tasks pay for themselves instantly.

Timeout and Error Handling

Agents sometimes timeout. Plan for it:

const runWithRetry = async (task: string, maxRetries = 2) => {
  for (let i = 0; i < maxRetries; i++) {
    try {
      return await agent.run(task);
    } catch (error) {
      if (error.code === 'TIMEOUT' && i < maxRetries - 1) {
        console.log(`Timeout on attempt ${i + 1}, retrying...`);
        await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2000));
      } else {
        throw error;
      }
    }
  }
};

Timeouts usually mean: the agent tried to run a 60+ second command (like a slow test). Give it a different approach or break the task into pieces.

Monitoring: Understand What Your Agent Did

Add logging to debug unexpected behavior:

const agent = new Agent({
  model: 'claude-opus-4-7',
  onTurnStart: (turn, state) => {
    console.log(`[Turn ${turn}] Next action...`);
  },
  onToolCall: (toolName, params) => {
    console.log(`[Tool] Running ${toolName}`);
  },
  onTurnEnd: (turn, result) => {
    console.log(`[Turn ${turn}] Result: ${result.substring(0, 100)}...`);
  },
});

This logging is invaluable when an agent does something unexpected. You can see exactly which turn and which tool call caused the issue. The Cursor SDK TypeScript docs provide more details on available logging hooks and debugging options.

Safety: Constrain What Agents Can Do

Production agents shouldn’t have write access to everything:

const agent = new Agent({
  allowedDirectories: ['src/', 'tests/'], // Only write here
  readOnlyDirectories: ['config/', '.git/', 'node_modules/'],
  forbiddenPatterns: ['process.exit', 'eval(', 'require('], // Dangerous code
});

Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Pitfall 1: Vague Prompts Lead to Wandering Agents

Agents follow your lead. Vague prompts make them explore aimlessly.

Bad:

await agent.run('Improve the code');

The agent reads a few files, makes some generic improvements, and gives up.

Good:

await agent.run(`
The search endpoint in src/api/search.ts is slow. 
Trace the database query and identify the bottleneck. 
Look for missing indexes, N+1 queries, or inefficient filtering. 
Then optimize with specific database changes.
`);

The agent has a roadmap and knows exactly what to investigate.

Pitfall 2: Scope Creep

Agents get confused by huge codebases. Focus them:

// ❌ Too broad
await agent.run('Review the whole application');

// ✅ Focused
await agent.run('Review src/components/auth/* for XSS vulnerabilities');

A 10-file codebase vs 100-file codebase makes a huge difference in agent accuracy.

Pitfall 3: Timeout Traps

60-second timeout catches agents trying to do too much:

// ❌ Might timeout (running entire test suite is slow)
await agent.run('Run all tests and fix failures');

// ✅ Safer (run specific tests)
await agent.run('Run tests for src/utils/* and fix any failures');

If an agent tries to run a slow process (build, test), give it a faster alternative or split the work.

Pitfall 4: Tool Parameter Confusion

Define tool schemas precisely:

// ❌ Unclear
const tool = {
  parameters: {
    path: { type: 'string' }, // What format? Absolute? Relative?
  },
};

// ✅ Clear
const tool = {
  parameters: {
    filePath: {
      type: 'string',
      description: 'Relative path from project root, e.g., "src/index.ts"',
    },
  },
};

The agent will call your tools more accurately if the schema is unambiguous.

Pitfall 5: Agents Can’t See Real-Time Changes

If you modify files while an agent is running, it won’t see them:

// You write to src/config.ts
await fs.writeFile('src/config.ts', newConfig);
// Agent has stale content
const old = await agent.readFile('src/config.ts'); // Gets old version

Agents only see what they read. If external code changes files, agents get stale state.

When to Use Agents in Your Workflow

Perfect use cases:

  • Generating documentation (JSDoc, README, API docs)
  • Adding tests to untested code
  • Refactoring large modules
  • Finding security/performance issues in code
  • Migrating code patterns (old API to new API)

Where they struggle:

  • Novel algorithm design (agents copy existing patterns)
  • Architectural decisions (needs human judgment)
  • Domain knowledge outside their training (they’ll guess)
  • Very tight latency requirements (less than 100ms)

The Future of Agents

Cursor Agents SDK is actively developed. Coming improvements might include:

  • Parallel tool execution (faster for independent tasks)
  • Longer timeouts for heavy operations
  • Better IDE integration (agents could use your current selection)
  • Custom model support

The framework is stable enough for production today, but these improvements will make agents faster and more capable.

Conclusion

Cursor Agents SDK is best understood as a smart automation tool for code-related tasks. It doesn’t replace developers, it amplifies them. A developer who knows how to direct agents effectively will be dramatically more productive than one using the SDK blindly.

Start small: Build a documentation agent, test it, validate the output. Then scale to more complex automation. Every agent you build teaches you patterns that apply to bigger problems.

The agents that succeed share one trait: crystal-clear instructions. Vague prompts produce vague results. Specific, detailed prompts produce reliable automation.

Ready to get started? The Cursor SDK documentation has everything you need to build production agents, and there are plenty of examples and tutorials available to learn from real-world use cases.

title: Ziegler-Nichols PID Tuning from First Principles: The Method That Brought Control Theory Out of the…
partialText:
Ziegler-Nichols PID Tuning from First Principles: The Method That Brought Control Theory Out of the Laboratory and Into the Factory

A complete engineering deep-dive into the Ziegler-Nichols step response and ultimate gain methods; the mathematics behind them, why they work, where they fail, and how to apply them to a real Arduino motor controller.

Introduction

In the comments section of my previous article on PID control, Tdperk; an industrial automation engineer with nearly thirty years of experience; made a point that deserves a full response rather than a paragraph. He noted, with considerable restraint, that a PID article which does not mention Ziegler-Nichols, Nichols, or Smith is something of an omission. He was right.

The previous article deliberately prioritised intuition over methodology; building understanding of what each PID term does physically before introducing formal mathematics. That was the correct decision for that audience. But an engineer who understands what PID does and has implemented it successfully is ready for the next question: how do you tune it properly, without guessing?

That is what this article answers. Ziegler-Nichols is not simply a formula to be looked up in a table. It is a principled methodology grounded in a specific model of how dynamic systems respond to inputs; and understanding the model is what allows you to use the method intelligently, recognise when it is appropriate, and diagnose why it fails when it does.

GitHub repository: github.com/MooMooCow29/Building-an-Arduino-Robot-Car

Part One: Why Empirical Tuning Is Not Enough

The previous article introduced a tuning procedure based on observation: increase Kp until the system oscillates, back off, add Ki until steady-state error disappears, optionally add a small Kd. This approach works; but it is not a method in the engineering sense. It produces different results depending on the engineer’s patience, the measurement conditions, and the specific disturbances present during testing.

Two engineers applying the same procedure to the same system will arrive at different gains. Neither can justify their choice analytically. Neither can predict how the system will behave under conditions different from those during tuning. This matters more than it might appear. A robot driving on a smooth floor may be tuned to perform well there; but when it encounters carpet, a slope, or a heavier payload, the plant dynamics change.

Ziegler-Nichols provides something better: a systematic procedure that characterises the dynamic behaviour of the plant through a small number of measurable quantities, then maps those quantities to gain values using relationships derived from control theory.

The Plant Model Assumption

All of Ziegler-Nichols is built on an assumption about the form of the plant’s transfer function. The method assumes the plant can be approximated as a first-order system with time delay; the FOPDT model:

G(s) = K × e^(-Ls) / (τs + 1)

Where:
  K  =  process gain
         (steady-state output per unit input)

  L  =  apparent dead time
         (delay before output begins to respond)

  τ  =  time constant
         (time to reach 63.2% of final value)

  s  =  Laplace variable

This is called the FOPDT model; First Order Plus Dead Time. It is a remarkably good approximation for a wide range of real processes; including motor speed control; even when the true system is more complex. The dead time L captures the combined effect of all delays in the system: sensor latency, computational delay, actuator response time, and physical inertia.

Part Two: The Step Response Method

Ziegler-Nichols published two tuning methods in their landmark 1942 paper. The first; the step response method; is an open-loop procedure. The second; the ultimate gain method; is a closed-loop procedure. We cover both, beginning with the step response.

Conducting the Step Response Test

The step response method characterises the plant by applying a step change to the input and observing the output. For the motor speed controller:

• Ensure the motor is at rest and all PID gains are set to zero (Kp = Ki = Kd = 0).

• Apply a step change to the PWM input; jumping from 0 to a fixed value, typically PWM 128 to 180.

• Record the motor speed (encoder pulses per 100ms window) at regular intervals until steady state.

  • Plot speed against time to obtain the characteristic S-shaped FOPDT response curve.

Extracting L, τ, and K from the Response Curve

From the step response curve, three quantities are extracted graphically. Draw a tangent to the steepest part of the S-curve. This tangent line intersects two reference levels:

Process Gain  K
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  K = (steady-state speed − initial speed)
      ──────────────────────────────────────
               step PWM value

  Example:  K = 9 / 180 = 0.05  pulses per PWM unit


Dead Time  L
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Where the tangent line crosses the baseline
  Typical range on TT motors:  100 – 200 ms


Time Constant  τ
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Time between tangent crossing final level and L
  Typical range on TT motors:  300 – 600 ms

Ziegler-Nichols Step Response Gain Formulas

P  controller
───────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  τ / (K × L)


PI  controller
───────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  0.9 × τ / (K × L)
  Ti  =  L / 0.3
  Ki  =  Kp / Ti


PID  controller
───────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  1.2 × τ / (K × L)
  Ti  =  2L          →   Ki  =  Kp / Ti
  Td  =  0.5L        →   Kd  =  Kp × Td

Worked Example on the Robot Motor

Suppose the step response test on the left motor produces the following measurements:

Inputs
───────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Step input            PWM  180
  Steady-state speed      9  pulses / 100 ms
  Dead time        L  =  0.15 s   (150 ms)
  Time constant    τ  =  0.40 s   (400 ms)
  Process gain     K  =  9 / 180  =  0.05


Applying the PID formulas
───────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  1.2 × τ / (K × L)
      =  1.2 × 0.40 / (0.05 × 0.15)
      =  0.48 / 0.0075
      =  64.0

  Ti  =  2L  =  2 × 0.15  =  0.30 s
  Ki  =  Kp / Ti  =  64.0 / 0.30  =  213.3

  Td  =  0.5L  =  0.5 × 0.15  =  0.075 s
  Kd  =  Kp × Td  =  64.0 × 0.075  =  4.8
These values are the Ziegler-Nichols starting point. They typically produce approximately 25% overshoot on a speed step change. For smoother response, reduce all three gains by 20–30% from these values.

Part Three: The Ultimate Gain Method

The second Ziegler-Nichols method is a closed-loop procedure. Rather than characterising the plant from an open-loop step response, it drives the closed-loop system to the boundary of instability and measures the characteristics of the resulting oscillation.

The Concept of Ultimate Gain

For a proportional-only controller (Ki = 0, Kd = 0), there exists a gain value Ku; the ultimate gain; at which the closed-loop system oscillates continuously with constant amplitude. Below Ku, oscillations decay and the system is stable. Above Ku, oscillations grow and the system is unstable. At exactly Ku, the system sustains a steady sinusoidal oscillation; a condition called marginal stability.

The period of this oscillation is the ultimate period Pu. Together, Ku and Pu characterise the closed-loop system’s dynamic behaviour and map directly to PID gains through the Ziegler-Nichols ultimate gain formulas.

Ultimate Gain Tuning Formulas

P  controller
───────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  0.5 × Ku


PI  controller
───────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  0.45 × Ku
  Ti  =  Pu / 1.2
  Ki  =  Kp / Ti


PID  controller
───────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  0.6  × Ku
  Ti  =  Pu / 2     →   Ki  =  Kp / Ti
  Td  =  Pu / 8     →   Kd  =  Kp × Td

Worked Example

Inputs
───────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Ultimate gain    Ku  =  35
  Ultimate period  Pu  =  0.5 s


Applying the PID formulas
───────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Kp  =  0.6  × 35        =  21.0

  Ti  =  0.5 / 2          =  0.25 s
  Ki  =  21.0 / 0.25      =  84.0

  Td  =  0.5 / 8          =  0.0625 s
  Kd  =  21.0 × 0.0625   =  1.3125

Step Response vs Ultimate Gain: Which to Use?

The step response method is safer; it requires no closed-loop oscillation and carries no risk of driving the system into instability during the test. The ultimate gain method tends to produce gains that are better tuned to the closed-loop dynamics; because it characterises the system in closed-loop rather than open-loop operation.

In practice: use the step response method first to get a working set of gains quickly, then use the ultimate gain method to refine if the response is not satisfactory.

Part Four: Arduino Implementation

The previous article’s PID implementation requires no structural changes to use Ziegler-Nichols gains. The only change is in config.h: replace the hand-tuned gain values with the Ziegler-Nichols derived values.

Step Response Test Sketch

/**
 * test_step_response.ino
 * Open-loop step response characterisation for Ziegler-Nichols tuning.
 * Send any character to Serial Monitor to trigger the step.
 * Copy printed CSV data into a spreadsheet and plot to extract L, tau, K.
 */

#define STEP_PWM           180
#define SAMPLE_INTERVAL_MS 100
#define RECORD_DURATION_MS 3000

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  motors_init();
  encoder_init();
  motors_stop();
  Serial.println(F("Send any key to begin"));
  while (!Serial.available()) {}
  Serial.println(F("time_ms,speed_L,speed_R"));
  unsigned long start = millis();
  motors_set(STEP_PWM, true, STEP_PWM, true);
  unsigned long lastSample = start;
  while (millis() - start < RECORD_DURATION_MS) {
    if (millis() - lastSample >= SAMPLE_INTERVAL_MS) {
      Serial.print(millis() - start); Serial.print(',');
      Serial.print(encoder_get_speed(MOTOR_LEFT)); Serial.print(',');
      Serial.println(encoder_get_speed(MOTOR_RIGHT));
      lastSample = millis();
    }
  }
  motors_stop();
  while(true) {}
}
void loop() {}

Part Five: Limitations of Ziegler-Nichols

Intellectual honesty demands that the limitations of this method be stated as clearly as its strengths. Ziegler-Nichols is old; published in 1942; and the intervening eight decades of control engineering research have produced a detailed understanding of exactly where and why it fails.

Designed for a Specific Objective Function

The Ziegler-Nichols formulas were derived to minimise the integral of the absolute error (IAE) following a step disturbance, producing a quarter-decay ratio response; fast, moderately oscillatory, and well-suited to the industrial process control applications of the 1940s. For motor speed control on a robot, the objective is different: smooth, consistent speed with minimal overshoot rather than aggressive disturbance rejection.

The practical fix: apply a detuning factor. Reduce Kp by 30%, Ki by 40%, and Kd by 20% from the Ziegler-Nichols values. This conservative variant trades response speed for smoothness.

Assumes a Linear, Time-Invariant Plant

The FOPDT model assumes that the plant behaves the same way regardless of operating point. Real motors are nonlinear: the relationship between PWM and speed is different at low speeds (where static friction dominates) versus high speeds (where back-EMF dominates). The process gain K measured at 50% PWM may differ significantly from K at 20% PWM.

This is one motivation for gain scheduling: computing different sets of gains for different operating regions and switching between them as the operating point changes. It is also one motivation for the more advanced control methods discussed in Part Six.

Derivative Filtering

The derivative term amplifies high-frequency noise in the measurement signal. The Ziegler-Nichols Kd values are often too large for encoder-based systems where the pulse count measurement is inherently discrete and noisy between windows. A derivative filter is standard practice in production implementations:

// First-order low-pass derivative filter
// α closer to 1 = more filtering, less noise, slower response
// α closer to 0 = less filtering, more noise, faster response
// Start with α = 0.8 and adjust empirically

float alpha = 0.8f;
filtered_D  = alpha * filtered_D_prev + (1.0f - alpha) * raw_D;

Part Six: Beyond Ziegler-Nichols

Tdperk raised two further topics in his comment that deserve direct engagement: feedforward control as a supplement to the integral term, and fuzzy logic as an alternative to classical PID. Both represent directions that classical Ziegler-Nichols tuning cannot address.

Feedforward Control

A PID controller is reactive: it responds to errors after they have occurred. Feedforward control is proactive: it uses knowledge of the system to generate a baseline control signal before any error has occurred. For motor speed control, the feedforward term is straightforward:

// Feedforward baseline from measured process gain K
// K = steady-state speed / step PWM  (from step response test)

float feedforward = setpoint / K;

// Add to PID output:
float output = feedforward + P + I + D;

// The PID then only corrects residual error,
// dramatically reducing integrator burden and settling time.
Feedforward is arguably the highest-value single improvement to the PID controller described in the previous article; providing a larger performance improvement per unit of implementation effort than any gain tuning refinement.

Fuzzy Logic Control

Fuzzy logic as a control strategy emerged prominently in the 1980s and 1990s as an alternative to classical PID for systems that are difficult to model analytically. Rather than computing a precise control output from a mathematical model, a fuzzy controller maps inputs (typically error and rate of change of error) to outputs through a set of linguistic rules:

IF error is LARGE_POSITIVE  AND rate is INCREASING  THEN output is VERY_HIGH
IF error is SMALL_NEGATIVE  AND rate is DECREASING  THEN output is SLIGHTLY_LOW
IF error is NEAR_ZERO       AND rate is STABLE      THEN output is UNCHANGED

The theoretical appeal of fuzzy logic for motor control is real: it can handle nonlinearities and operating-point variations more gracefully than a linear PID with fixed gains, without requiring an explicit plant model. In practice, however, the tuning of membership functions is itself an empirical process; and for well-behaved systems like DC motor speed control, a properly tuned PID with feedforward performs comparably or better with significantly less implementation complexity.

The Smith Predictor and Cohen-Coon

The Smith Predictor; proposed by O.J.M. Smith in 1957; addresses one of the most challenging problems in process control: systems with large dead times relative to their time constants. When L/τ is large (greater than approximately 0.5), Ziegler-Nichols performance degrades significantly.

The Smith Predictor resolves this by using a model of the dead-time-free plant within the control loop, effectively removing the dead time from the feedback path. For motor speed control, L/τ is typically around 0.375; below the threshold where the Smith Predictor becomes necessary. But knowing it exists; knowing that dead-time compensation is a distinct and solved problem in control theory; is part of being a complete control engineer.

Cohen-Coon is a step response tuning method like Ziegler-Nichols but with improved performance specifically for processes with large dead times (L/τ > 0.3). It is the appropriate alternative to Ziegler-Nichols when the step response test reveals a large apparent dead time.

Conclusion: Tuning Is System Identification in Disguise

The deeper insight that emerges from studying Ziegler-Nichols properly is that tuning a PID controller is fundamentally an exercise in system identification. Before you can tune a controller, you must characterise the plant. The step response test and the ultimate gain test are both system identification procedures; they extract the key parameters of the plant’s dynamic behaviour and map them to controller gains through a model-based relationship.

This is why engineers with deep control theory backgrounds approach tuning differently from those who have only ever tuned empirically. They think about the plant first: what is its gain, its time constant, its dead time? Is the FOPDT model a reasonable approximation? The answers to these questions determine not just what gain values to use, but which tuning method is appropriate and what level of performance is achievable.

Ziegler and Nichols gave engineers a practical, systematic answer to a question that had previously been answered only by intuition and experience. Their 1942 paper remained standard practice in industrial control for decades and still forms the foundation of most introductory control engineering curricula. Understanding it properly; not just as a formula to be applied, but as a methodology grounded in a specific plant model and a specific performance objective; is the difference between an engineer who can tune a system and one who can only copy the gains someone else found.
